orient: Narrator: Nelly Dean, still telling Lockwood her story. It is a few months after Heathcliff's return, in the frosty winter of 1783–84, and Heathcliff is still visiting the Grange. Nelly opens with a walk she took past Wuthering Heights, which she left with Catherine about ten months earlier.

notes.n: A bonnet was a woman's hat framing the face and tied under the chin.
Nelly thinks of the Heights as a working farm, which it is.

notes.t: warn him how people talked regarding his ways
notes.g: Warn Hindley about the gossip on his way of life.
notes.n: Hindley's drinking and gambling with Heathcliff (Chapter X).

notes.t: doubting if I could bear to be taken at my word
notes.g: Unsure I could face it if I actually had to go through with it.

notes.t: about the period that my narrative has reached
notes.g: Around the point I've reached in my story.

notes.t: the highway branches off on to the moor
notes.g: The main road splits, with a track leading up onto the open moor.
Wuthering Heights. 'G.' is Gimmerton and 'T. G.' is Thrushcross Grange.
notes.n: Each letter is carved on the side facing that place.

notes.g: A rush of feelings from childhood.
Hindley Earnshaw, Catherine's brother, master of Wuthering Heights.
notes.n: Nelly's mother nursed him, so they were playmates as small children (Chapter IV).

notes.g: Thought of it as a favourite place.
Things that would rot or spoil, like food.
A flat chip of grey stone.

notes.t: supposing it were a sign of death
notes.g: What if it were an omen of death?
notes.n: In folk belief, seeing a vision of a living person could be a warning that they would soon die.

notes.g: The ghostly figure had got there before me.

notes.n: Knots in hair were once blamed on elves tangling it at night.

notes.g: Hareton Earnshaw, Hindley's little son, now about six.
notes.n: Nelly looked after him from babyhood, after his mother died (Chapter VIII), and had to leave him when she went to the Grange (Chapter IX).
'Thee', 'thou' and 'thy' were the familiar forms of 'you' and 'your', used with children and family.

notes.m: A 'nurse' here was a woman who looked after a child, not a medical nurse.

notes.g: A hard stone with sharp edges.
The force of someone used to swearing.
Spite; a wish to do harm.

notes.n: Oranges were an imported treat, especially in winter in a remote place.

notes.g: Win him over; calm him down.

notes.n: When Nelly left, Hindley said the curate would take Hareton in hand and teach him (Chapter IX).

notes.m: 'Master' here means a schoolmaster or teacher, not a boss.

notes.g: Hareton's muddled answer: his teacher is his devil of a father.
notes.n: Nelly's next questions try to untangle it: the devil, or Daddy?
'Gait' is the northern word 'gate', meaning way or path.

notes.tr: I don't know. He pays Dad back for what Dad gives me: he curses Daddy for cursing me. He says I must do whatever I like.

notes.g: The dashes stand for swear words Nelly won't repeat.
notes.n: Printers of the time used dashes in place of bad language.

notes.g: The stone slabs at the front doorstep.

notes.t: as if I had raised a goblin
notes.g: As if I had conjured up an evil spirit.
Isabella Linton, Edgar's sister, who has fallen for Heathcliff (Chapter X).
Blocking; getting in the way of.
Isabella, the young lady of the house.
Showing her any politeness he didn't have to.

notes.t: a sweeping survey of the house-front
notes.g: A quick look all along the front of the house (to check no one was watching).

notes.m: Not a sidewalk by a street: the stone paving of the courtyard.

notes.n: Judas Iscariot betrayed Jesus with a kiss, which is why the name springs to Nelly's lips at this embrace.

notes.m: 'Ejaculate' meant to cry out suddenly. No sexual meaning.

notes.g: Courting Isabella; saying loving things to her.
notes.m: 'Making love' meant flirting or wooing with words. No sexual meaning.

notes.t: giving some loose to my indignation
notes.g: Letting out some of my anger.

notes.t: You want setting down in your right place
notes.g: You need putting back in your place.

notes.t: wish Linton to draw the bolts against you
notes.g: Want Edgar to bolt the doors to keep you out.
notes.n: Catherine often calls her husband by his surname, 'Linton'.

notes.t: Every day I grow madder after sending him to heaven
notes.g: Every day I'm more desperate to kill him.
I'm protective of you and your interests.
notes.n: Jealous 'for' someone means anxious on their behalf, not envious.

notes.g: Edgar Linton, master of Thrushcross Grange.
Put up with it without taking revenge.

notes.t: The tyrant grinds down his slaves and they don’t turn against him; they crush those beneath them
notes.g: People who are crushed don't strike back at the strong; they take it out on someone weaker.
notes.n: Heathcliff says he won't take revenge on Catherine herself.

notes.t: Having levelled my palace, don’t erect a hovel
notes.g: Having destroyed my happiness, don't offer me a miserable substitute.
notes.n: A 'hovel' is a wretched little hut. He means her offer of Isabella as a wife.

notes.t: as bad as offering Satan a lost soul
notes.g: Like handing a soul over to the Devil to torment.
notes.n: Catherine means Isabella would only be a victim for him.

notes.t: restless to know us at peace
notes.g: Unable to bear knowing we are at peace.

notes.t: the most efficient method of revenging yourself on me
notes.g: The most effective way to get revenge on me.
Red in the face and in a dark mood.

notes.t: she could neither lay nor control it
notes.g: Like a magician who has called up a spirit she can't control or send back.
notes.n: To 'lay' a ghost or spirit means to make it rest. Catherine has stirred up passions she can no longer settle.

notes.g: On the stone floor in front of the fireplace.

notes.t: assuming the defensive for her guest
Call me two men out of the hall
notes.g: Fetch me two of the menservants.
notes.n: Probably the servants' hall, where the staff ate and gathered. Edgar means to have Heathcliff thrown out.

notes.g: I have given in to her enough.
notes.m: To 'humour' someone is to indulge them, nothing to do with comedy.

notes.n: Pronounced 'BLAG-erd'.

notes.m: 'Calculated' here means intended, not worked out with numbers.

notes.g: Refuse to let you in from now on.
Make it forced and humiliating (you will be thrown out).

notes.t: this lamb of yours threatens like a bull
notes.g: Your gentle little husband is making big threats.

notes.m: 'Signed' here means made a sign or gesture, not wrote a signature.

notes.t: feigning more valour than you possess
notes.g: Pretending to be braver than you are.

notes.t: For his life he could not avert
In old days this would win you knighthood
notes.g: Sarcastic: in the age of chivalry such 'bravery' would make you a knight.
A baby hare still drinking its mother's milk.
Sarcastic: enjoy him, if you can.
Weak coward, with milk for blood.

notes.t: You’ve played me an ill turn

notes.g: Cornered and fighting back, like a hunted animal.
Like a nut whose shell crumbles easily.

notes.t: framing a bit of a lie
the coachman and the two gardeners
notes.n: A gentry house like the Grange kept a sizeable staff.

notes.g: Three servants; people of lower rank.
The iron rod for stirring the fire.
I'm nearly out of my mind.
notes.m: 'Distracted' meant frantic, driven half mad, not just unable to concentrate.

notes.g: I would throw accusations back at him.

notes.n: Originally a military term for a band of soldiers sent first into a near-hopeless attack.

notes.t: represent the peril of quitting that policy
notes.g: Explain the danger of changing that approach.
Close to madness once it is lit.

notes.t: turning of her fits of passion to account
notes.g: Using her outbursts to get her own way.

notes.t: neither come to wrangle nor be reconciled
notes.g: Here neither to argue nor to make up.

notes.m: 'Intimacy' meant close friendship, with no sexual sense.

notes.g: Locking it to keep me out.
Sharply, in a way that allowed no argument.
The midday meal and the afternoon meal.
notes.m: 'Dinner' was the main meal, eaten around midday; 'tea' came later in the day.

notes.g: End his questioning without getting anywhere.
End all family ties between them.
